title: Leuprorelin 22.5 mg: hormone injection every 12 weeks
context_label: Advanced disease, or selected high-risk disease with radiotherapy
indication_text: Hormone-dependent advanced prostate cancer, or high-risk localised/locally advanced hormone-dependent disease in combination with radiotherapy.
purpose: This is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): it lowers testosterone to help control prostate cancer. With radiotherapy, the aim may be cure; in advanced disease, it is part of ongoing cancer control.
schedule_summary: Leuprorelin 22.5 mg is injected under the skin every 12 weeks (84 days) in this NCCP regimen. The prescribed duration depends on whether it supports radiotherapy or treats advanced disease.
administration_text: A trained healthcare professional prepares and gives this specific formulation under the skin. Correct mixing and administration matter for hormone suppression. Different leuprorelin products and strengths have different instructions; they must not be substituted by matching the number of milligrams alone.
monitoring_summary: Repeat blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and bone blood profile when clinically indicated. PSA and testosterone assess response. A suspected preparation or administration problem needs review and a testosterone check.

agents.name: Leuprorelin 22.5 mg
agents.mechanism: Reduces testosterone through sustained pituitary stimulation
agents.explanation: Leuprorelin is a GnRH agonist. Testosterone can rise briefly at the start before continued stimulation switches down the pituitary signal. The depot then maintains suppression between injections. The team assesses flare protection and confirms that testosterone is adequately suppressed.
agents.watch: Confirm the exact next injection date. With radiotherapy, ask when hormone treatment starts and ends and how the radiotherapy dates fit. A low PSA does not mean you should stop injections. Tell the team about worsening pain, trouble passing urine or severe headache with vision changes.
risks: Hot flushes, sweating, fatigue and changes in sleep or mood
Reduced sex drive, erection difficulties and reduced fertility
Loss of bone strength, fracture risk, muscle loss and changes in weight
Changes in glucose, cholesterol and cardiovascular risk
Heart-rhythm changes; review other medicines that affect the QT interval
Initial flare with worsening bone pain or urinary obstruction
Injection-site pain or reactions; incorrect preparation can reduce efficacy
Depression, allergic reactions and rare raised pressure around the brain

phases_note: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) lowers testosterone, a hormone that can drive prostate cancer. This medicine is your ADT. Additional cancer tablets, chemotherapy or radiotherapy are separate decisions based on your cancer and overall health. Keep treatment going until your team changes the plan; do not stop because prostate-specific antigen (PSA) has fallen.

anatomy: Report severe low mood, marked fatigue or sleep problems. Ask for support early.
Hormone suppression can cause hot flushes. Ask about practical measures and treatments if troublesome.
Keep planned checks. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness needs urgent assessment.
Blood glucose, weight and cardiovascular risk need review; suitable activity and diet can help.
Report worsening redness, swelling, severe pain or a persistent reaction.
Reduced desire and erection difficulties are common. Discuss fertility and contraception; ADT is not reliable contraception.
Ask about bone assessment, resistance exercise, falls prevention, calcium intake and vitamin D needs.
Report difficulty passing urine or worsening pain. New leg weakness or loss of bladder/bowel control is an emergency.

support.title: Sickness support
support.text: This treatment has minimal sickness risk. Routine preventive anti-sickness medicines are not usually required; agree a plan if symptoms develop.

support.title: Bone and muscle health
support.text: Discuss fracture risk, bone-density testing when indicated, calcium intake, vitamin D and suitable resistance and aerobic exercise. Supplements and bone medicines are individual decisions.

support.title: Sexual health, mood and hot flushes
support.text: Tell the team which effects matter most. Support is available for sexual function, sleep, mood and vasomotor symptoms.

items.text: This is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): it lowers testosterone to help control prostate cancer. With radiotherapy, the aim may be cure; in advanced disease, it is part of ongoing cancer control.

items.title: Additional treatment
items.text: In metastatic hormone-sensitive cancer, many suitable patients benefit from an additional androgen-pathway medicine, and sometimes chemotherapy. Radiotherapy can have a different role in localised disease, selected metastatic disease or symptom relief. Your specialist explains the options for your setting.

items.title: Deciding together
items.text: Discuss expected benefit, uncertainty, side effects, alternatives including surgical castration where appropriate, and the option of declining treatment. No one duration fits every setting.

evidence.title: What the evidence can tell you
evidence.intro: Trials support the discussion but do not predict an individual outcome.
evidence.population: Hormone-dependent advanced prostate cancer, or high-risk localised/locally advanced hormone-dependent disease in combination with radiotherapy.
evidence.comparison: Disease setting and local treatment determine the relevant comparator
evidence.interpretation: For selected high-risk localised or locally advanced prostate cancer, ADT is combined with radiotherapy to improve cancer control. In advanced disease it forms the hormone-treatment foundation. Duration and additional medicines depend on the setting; this information does not establish one universal course or a survival ranking among depot products.
limitations: Hormone suppression is a different endpoint from survival.
Choice depends on disease setting, adherence, interactions, comorbidity and patient priorities; do not rank products using separate trials.

consent_support: Discuss treatment aim, duration, benefits and uncertainty, alternatives, sexual health and fertility, hot flushes, fatigue, mood, bone and muscle effects, metabolic/cardiovascular risks, interactions, formulation-specific risks, tests and urgent contacts. Tell the team about worsening pain, trouble passing urine or severe headache with vision changes.

questions.q: What is the aim and how long is this planned for?
questions.a: This is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): it lowers testosterone to help control prostate cancer. With radiotherapy, the aim may be cure; in advanced disease, it is part of ongoing cancer control.

questions.q: Do I need another cancer medicine or radiotherapy alongside this?
questions.a: Ask how this hormone treatment fits the plan for your disease. Additional hormone-pathway medicines, chemotherapy and radiotherapy have different roles; they are not automatically needed in every setting.

questions.q: When is my next dose and what if I miss it?
questions.a: Confirm the exact next injection date. With radiotherapy, ask when hormone treatment starts and ends and how the radiotherapy dates fit. A low PSA does not mean you should stop injections. Tell the team about worsening pain, trouble passing urine or severe headache with vision changes.

questions.q: How can we protect bone, heart, sexual and mental health?
questions.a: Ask for a plan covering exercise, bone and fracture risk, blood pressure and glucose, sexual symptoms, mood and sleep. Tell the team about changes early so support can be offered.

Use the verified daytime and out-of-hours numbers supplied by your treating hospital. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, a seizure or severe chest pain, call 112 or 999. Do not use the example numbers in this draft.
